In the 12 months to August 2023, 112,418 people died of a drug overdose in the United States. In the 12 months to June 2026, the latest CDC figure, it was 65,724. That is 41.5% lower, about 46,700 fewer deaths a year, and the lowest count since the end of 2016. The 12-month count has now fallen for 34 months in a row.

That national curve is well covered. I wanted to know what it looks like underneath: did every state turn at the same time?

**The short answer: no. The decline started in West Virginia and Ohio in 2021 and moved west.** Most of the East and Midwest peaked in 2021–23, the West Coast in early 2024, Arizona in late 2025, and New Mexico's count is the highest it has ever been. But the more interesting part is the timing. Fentanyl took about eight years to spread from New England to Nevada, and the peaks came much closer together than that. The West didn't have to wait its turn.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The data.** CDC's provisional drug overdose death counts (National Vital Statistics System), downloaded in November 2026. Each figure is a count of deaths over the previous 12 months, published monthly from January 2015 to June 2026. I use CDC's "predicted" counts, which correct for death certificates still under investigation. 50 states plus DC; New York City is reported separately and I added it back to New York State.
:::

## The national picture

```{=html}
{{< include figures/od1_national.html >}}
```

Figure 1. Drug overdose deaths in the United States over the previous 12 months. Use the tabs to split by drug or by region. The drug categories overlap: a death involving both fentanyl and methamphetamine counts in both lines.

The fall is led by fentanyl. Deaths involving synthetic opioids (in practice, illicit fentanyl) are down 57% from their peak, from 78,300 to 33,900 a year. Deaths involving methamphetamine and other stimulants are down 35%, and cocaine 38%. At the peak, fentanyl was involved in 70% of all overdose deaths; now it's 52%.

The third tab shows the first sign that this isn't one national story. In 2023 the four regions were close together, between 31 and 36 deaths per 100,000 people. Since then the Northeast, Midwest and South have fallen to 16–18. The West is at 25.7. It had the lowest rate in the country in 2019 and has the highest now.

## Not everywhere at once

For each state I took the month when its 12-month count was highest, looking from 2019 onwards so that the fentanyl-era wave is what gets measured.

```python
era = deaths.loc["2019":]          # 12-month counts, one column per state
peak = era.idxmax()                # when each state's count was highest
below = 100 * (1 - era.iloc[-1] / era.max())
```

```{=html}
{{< include figures/od2_map.html >}}
```

Figure 2. When each state's 12-month overdose count peaked (darker is later), how far below that peak it is now, and how it changed over the last 12 months. Hover for the numbers. DC is too small to see; it peaked in September 2023 and is 50% below.

- **Appalachia turned first.** West Virginia and Ohio peaked in the 12 months to April 2021, Maryland and Kentucky later that year. West Virginia has gone from 89 deaths per 100,000 people to 36.
- **Most of the country followed within two and a half years.** 44 of the 51 peaked between April 2021 and September 2023.
- **The West came last.** Washington and Oregon peaked in early 2024, Utah, Alaska and Nevada in mid-2024, and Arizona only in October 2025.
- **How far a state has fallen follows the same map.** 22 states are now at least 50% below their peak, and all but one (Oregon, with a caveat below) are east of the Rockies. The median Western state is 19% below its peak; the median state elsewhere is 51% below.

Longitude and peak date are clearly related (Spearman correlation −0.47 across the 51): on average a state 10 degrees further west peaked about three months later. It's a tendency, not a rule. Longitude explains under a quarter of the variation, and Colorado and Montana peaked early for the West.

```{=html}
{{< include figures/od3_wave.html >}}
```

Figure 3. Every state from east (top) to west (bottom), month by month since 2019. Each row is coloured by how close the state was to its own peak; the white dot marks the peak. The dark band drifts to the right going down the chart, and the pale area on the right, where deaths have fallen furthest, thins out towards the bottom.

## Fentanyl arrived years apart. The peaks didn't

Illicit fentanyl reached US drug markets from the east. To put a date on it for each state, I took the first 12-month window in which synthetic opioids were involved in at least half of the state's overdose deaths.

```python
share = fentanyl / deaths          # by state and month
arrival = (share >= 0.5).idxmax()  # first window where it reaches half
```

That date can be measured for 35 states. Ten others don't have usable drug-level data early enough, and in six (Hawaii, Iowa, Nebraska, South Dakota, Texas and Utah) fentanyl never reached half.

```{=html}
{{< include figures/od4_arrival.html >}}
```

Figure 4. For 35 states: when fentanyl was first involved in half of overdose deaths, against when overdose deaths peaked. The diagonal lines show a peak 0, 3 and 6 years after arrival. New Mexico's "peak" is simply the latest month of data.

If each state's epidemic had run its own course, the way an outbreak grows until it runs out of people to infect, the points would sit along one diagonal: arrive six years later, peak six years later. They don't.

- Fentanyl crossed the halfway mark in New Hampshire in early 2015 and in Nevada in mid-2023, **more than eight years apart**. The middle half of the states are spread over 4.6 years.
- The peaks of those same states are spread over **1.3 years**.
- In the 12 states where fentanyl arrived before 2018, deaths peaked a median of **5.8 years** later. In the 15 where it arrived in 2021 or later, **1.2 years** later.
- Put as a slope: a state where fentanyl arrived a year later peaked only about two months later.

So the wave took eight years to cross the country, but it crested almost everywhere within about three. That points to something that changed for the whole country around 2022–23, on top of each state's own epidemic. Researchers have put forward several candidates: naloxone became much more widely available (it has been sold over the counter since 2023), treatment expanded, the fentanyl supply itself appears to have changed, and in the hardest-hit places many of the people most at risk had already died. This analysis can't tell those apart. What it does say is that "each state just had to wait for its epidemic to burn out" doesn't fit the timing.

## Where it isn't falling

- **New Mexico** is the exception. Its 12-month count fell to 794 at the end of 2024, then rose to 1,152 by June 2026, up 32% in a year and the highest on record. At 54 deaths per 100,000 people, it now has the highest rate of any state.
- **Colorado** is up 13% over the last year (1,647 to 1,865) and only 5% below its 2022 peak.
- **Arizona** is 7% below a peak it reached only last October.
- Nebraska and Wyoming also show increases, but on 171 and 92 deaths a year, where a handful of cases moves the percentage.

All of these are in or next to the Southwest, so the wave hasn't finished moving.

## What it can't say

- **Provisional data.** Recent months get revised as death investigations close, and the predicted counts are CDC's estimate of where they will land. Oregon is the clearest case: its latest reported count is 535 and the predicted one is 758, so its 45% fall over the last year should be read with care.
- **12-month windows blur the timing.** A rolling count peaks when a month comes in lower than the same month a year before, which is some time after monthly deaths actually start to fall. That shifts every state the same way, so the order is preserved, but "peaked in April 2021" doesn't mean deaths started falling that month.
- **Drug categories are imperfect.** "Synthetic opioids" is mostly fentanyl but not only, and the shares depend on death certificates naming the drugs involved, which some states did poorly in the early years. The 50% threshold is my choice; it gives one date per state, not a full picture of how fentanyl spread.
- **State averages.** A state can be falling overall while one city or one group is not.
- **Timing, not causes.** The east-to-west pattern and the bunched-up peaks are descriptions. They narrow down which explanations are plausible; they don't prove any of them.

## Related

Asking *when* each curve turned, not just how high it went, is the same idea as the early- and late-decline groups in [my master's thesis on HIV in Sub-Saharan Africa](../hiv-ssa-thesis/). For why an epidemic that runs its own course peaks when it does, see the [epidemic modelling series](../epidemic-modelling/).
